feedback: 'What ONE quantity is this point?' — answers that only recount marks have missed the goal.
If the wrong number of partitions appears (e.g. four hash marks for fourths): 'How many equal parts, and how many marks between 0 and 1 does that take?'
Praise answers that name the point as a single magnitude and justify the number of marks.
activities.intendedInsight: A point on the line names one quantity; the numerator and denominator together specify a single number, and partitioning into n equal parts needs n−1 interior marks.
learnerActions: Start from a number line with only its endpoints (0 and 1) marked — no interior tick marks.
Cut the space from 0 to 1 into the number of equal parts needed for the fraction you want (e.g. four parts for fourths).
Say how many marks you had to add between 0 and 1 and why that many (fourths need three interior marks).
Point to the exact spot for the fraction and state what single amount that point represents — do not just count marks.
activities.title: Partition an unmarked line and name the quantity

feedback: If the child grabs the visible numbers or computes left-to-right: 'Which quantity is the whole here? Map the bar before writing the equation.'
If units are dropped or mismatched: 'Put the unit back on each number and convert to one unit first — what does 3/4 of a metre measure in cm?' (3/4 m = 75 cm).
Check units match (metres vs centimetres) before combining — convert and name both quantities, so 245 cm and 3/4 m are expressed in the same unit, then subtract (170 cm).
Reward explanations that tie each symbol to the story and that identify whole vs part correctly.
activities.intendedInsight: Equations should be structurally faithful to the situation — each number carries a referent and unit, quantities must share a unit before combining, and '=' means 'the same amount as', not 'compute left to right'.
learnerActions: Read a measurement or money story, e.g. 'A ribbon is 245 cm long; 3/4 of a metre is cut off.'
Draw a bar model that shows the whole, the parts, and where the unknown sits.
Before combining any numbers, convert so every quantity is in the SAME unit — e.g. 3/4 of a metre = 75 cm — so you are not subtracting 3/4 from 245.

Write a matching equation in which each number keeps its referent and a unit, using the common unit you converted to (for this ribbon, every quantity in cm, e.g. 245 cm − 75 cm = ? cm; use £ or pence consistently when the story is about money).
Say aloud what each number in the equation points back to in the situation, then solve using the bar (245 cm − 75 cm = 170 cm).
Translate in both directions: given an equation, describe the story and draw its bar; given a story, write the equation.
activities.title: Build a bar model and equation for a money/measurement story, units attached
